defects.summary: On the TCP transport a node mounting while its peer is up waits a full BAST period, about 10 s, for its EX request on the root directory inode (ino 128), because the peer holds the root at PR (cached, state GRANTED) and its release only arrives on the next BAST cycle; the mount therefore takes 10 s longer than the operation costs. A file read on the rejoined node also waited 1.56 s on a PR acquire in the same laps. Nothing hangs and nothing shuts down; this is pace, not stability, and does not block the 2-node TCP release bar.
defects.evidence: Measured 2026-09-13 on 0.85.5 module 45B8EB0F812B0167A4CCF9E, 2 nodes/TCP, during the D-0966 verification laps (tests/d0952_sole_create_rejoin_coherency.sh s617a-s617e): test2 (mounting/rejoining) dmesg at 7380 and 7471: P-LKTIMEOUT-HOLDER type=1 ino=128 ag=0 holder=<test1 id> hmode=PR hstate=2 held_ms=1046, 2070, ... 10262 queued_ms same (we=<test2 id> req=EX) once per second for 10 s, then P36-STACK ino=128 type=1 ag=0 mode=EX comm=mount (first timeout, dumping wait site) and P34-ACQ-SLOW ino=128 isdir=1 req_mode=5 dur_ms=10288 attempts=1 rc=0; and at 7431 P36-STACK ino=8388753 type=1 ag=0 mode=PR comm=cat then P34-ACQ-SLOW ino=8388753 isdir=0 req_mode=3 dur_ms=1560 attempts=1 rc=0. 12 P36-RETRY lines on test2 in that window. The lap consoles record B_MOUNT_RC=0 PHASE3 wall=4-5 s for the in-lap rejoin, so the 10 s waits fall in the cold-check remounts or the prep; the timestamps are in the test2 ring (uptime 2h at 07:13 UTC) and not yet in a per-lap capture.
defects.next: 1) Capture the survivor's side of the 10 s window: which BAST the root PR release answers (P-DIRBAST/P70-BP for ino=128 on test1 around the peer's mount) and why the first BAST does not release a cached, uncontended PR at once (a demote-on-first-BAST for the root should cost milliseconds). 2) Read mount's root EX request: whether it needs EX at all (upstream reads the root inode; the EX is MXFS's) and whether a PR would do. 3) Fix at the proven cause, then measure mount wall with a mounted peer before/after on the same build; budget the mount at 2x the lone mount. ===== ===== 2026-10-16, 0.90.131 build 6E5A99A6453278DB9F6CA5C, 2/net/mesh/direct g2: NOT REPRODUCED WITH A WITNESS, NOT DISPOSED. tests/rejoin_mount_wall.sh rmw3 (peer test1 stats and lists the root, test2 unmounts and mounts; P34-ACQ-SLOW enabled on test2 and P-DIRBAST on test1 by dynamic debug): 8 of 8 laps the peer logged P-DIRBAST ino=128 during the rejoiner's mount (so its cached root grant was asked for), the rejoiner logged no P34-ACQ-SLOW for ino 128 (no root acquire of 1 s or more; the record: 10288 ms), mounts 5.06-5.18 s. tests/agbast_mount_park.sh ap3 (both nodes mount at the same instant, 10 laps): no notification parked, no root acquire of 1 s or more, mounts 0.3-5.2 s. The cause of the 2026-09-13 waits was never established (the record's step 1 is still open), so which change removed it is not known; a candidate is the 0.90.20 parking of notifications that reach a mount before its handlers (the 10 s is the master's re-send period, and the record's waits fell in prep / cold-check remounts where both nodes mount). Next: reproduce the original shape on 0.85.5 module 45B8EB0F812B0167A4CCF9E with tests/d0952_sole_create_rejoin_coherency.sh to pin the cause, or show the park counters cover it.
defects.impact_why: Pace: the mount's root EX waited one BAST period (P34-ACQ-SLOW ino=128 dur_ms=10288 attempts=1 rc=0) and a read waited 1.56 s (rc=0); B_MOUNT_RC=0 on every lap, nothing hung or shut down. The record's own summary states it is pace, not stability.

defects.summary: The survivor's recovery completion still holds P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE and the exclusive-write gate behind mxfs_dlm_ledger_purge_owner, a SERIAL PER-PAGE durable pass over every page holding a record of the dead owner, measured at 4.6 ms a page: 4869 candidate pages took 22.4 s. Unlike the page takeover that used to sit next to it, this purge IS safety-required inside the barrier — the held-failure gate must see its result before the dead slot is republished, because a slot-indexed shared bit would otherwise alias to the slot's next occupant — so it cannot simply be deferred. Its cost is proportional to workload residue exactly as the takeover's was, so the same aged filesystem that produced a 7984-page takeover will produce a purge of the same order. SEPARATELY OBSERVED IN THE SAME WINDOW AND NOT YET EXPLAINED: two whole-ledger purges of the SAME {node, slot} ran concurrently and completed 18 microseconds apart with overlapping candidate sets (cand=4869 cleared=3650 total_ms=22443, and cand=4098 cleared=2439 total_ms=19096), so roughly 19 s of the 22.4 s may be duplicated work by two threads rather than one pass that is simply large.
defects.evidence: MEASURED 2/tcp on build E0970E5371DE62670F7994D, tests/d0962_takeover_offpath.sh ARM=control s40ctl (12000 creates of residue on the victim, then a virsh-destroy death lap). Survivor test1: 'foreign replay of slot 1 complete' at 919.226, P234-RECOV-STAGE 3->4 and 4->6 at 919.250/919.252, P-COMPLETE-RETIRE-TIMING slot=1 why=recovery-complete refresh_ms=1 ledger_ms=22443 dlmpurge_ms=0 handoff_ms=71148 at 1012.843, P-COMPLETE-TIMING disklock_purge_ms=640 at 1013.483, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE at 1013.484, P-PR-GATE-RESTORED at 1013.504. The 94.26 s the returning victim waited out decomposes exactly: 1 ms refresh + 22443 ms ledger purge + 0 dlm purge + 71148 ms page takeover + 640 ms disklock purge. The two purge lines: 'P-TAUTH-PURGE node=2366797610 slot=1 cleared=3650 pages=26426 cand=4869 bad=0 notmine=4785 visited=4869 selective=0 scan_ms=8 total_ms=22443' at 941.694927 and 'cleared=2439 cand=4098 visited=4098 scan_ms=256 total_ms=19096' at 941.694945. Evidence: tests/evidence/20260917T200133Z_d0962offpath_s40ctl. FOUND while verifying the takeover deferral: with the takeover off the critical path this purge is what is left holding the barrier.
defects.next: MORE EVIDENCE 2026-09-18 (s58h, 0.87.19): two healthy gate laps lost their mount to this purge on the recovery critical path. d0521_own_slice_cross_stamp_probe (whole-cluster crash, both slots dead): test1's rejoin ADMITTED at 23:42:33, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE slot=0 23:43:44, P163-RECOVERED slot=1 23:43:48 'running deferred local purge', then ~3400 purge lines until the harness's 90 s JOIN_BOUND killed the mount at 23:43:59 (MOUNT_RC=124 WALL_MS=94028; tests/evidence/20260918T233804Z_d0521_.../A_journal.txt). d0940_unknown_blocker_probe: same shape, recovered 23:50:13, killed 23:50:21 (MOUNT_RC=124 WALL_MS=91830; tests/evidence/20260918T234511Z_d0940_.../A_journal.txt). Both harnesses bound the join at 90 s (18x healthy) by their headers; the purge, not the replay, is what exceeds it. Previous next steps stand.
defects.impact_why: Pace: the purge completes and recovery completes behind it (s40ctl: ledger_ms=22443 inside a 94.26 s barrier that decomposes exactly, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE at 1013.484, P-PR-GATE-RESTORED 20 ms later). The s58h losses were the harnesses' 90 s join bound killing mount(8) while the purge was still running (MOUNT_RC=124), a budget failure, not a hang: the cost is proportional to residue and bounded by it. Nothing corrupted, crashed or shut down. A purge that fails to complete would be new evidence and re-adjudicates this.

defects.summary: Every persistent-reservation command wrapper in pal/linux/kern.c retries a UNIT ATTENTION and then discards it: the sense data is never classified and nothing is signalled upward. A target raises UA on the other initiators precisely to tell them the PR state they believe in has changed (SPC-4: 2Ah/03h RESERVATIONS PREEMPTED, 2Ah/04h RESERVATIONS RELEASED, 2Ah/05h REGISTRATIONS PREEMPTED, 29h/xx POWER ON or RESET). MXFS throws that notification away and waits for its own next scheduled poll, so a node that is not the elected PR-health maintainer learns of a reservation loss only at its slow audit -- and that interval is time the cluster cannot fence a peer death. The sess381 design ruling required event-driven checks 'at mount, on any unmount anomaly, on a target reset / Unit Attention, and unconditionally in the fencing path before a PREEMPT'; the UA trigger is the one item of that list never built.
defects.evidence: CODE FACT, verifiable by grep: 'grep -n UNIT_ATTENTION pal/linux/kern.c' returns a separate bounded retry loop per command -- the PR OUT preempt-and-abort path ~3756, REPORT CAPABILITIES ~3842, the PR IN wrappers ~4551 and ~4984, and the data-path READ passthrough ~683 and ~1379. Each tests only sense_key == UNIT_ATTENTION, sleeps and reissues; none reads asc/ascq, and no classification of asc/ascq for PR purposes exists anywhere in the tree. There is no single PAL funnel for PR commands, so the retry loops are per-command; and dlm/ must still build in user mode, so any signal has to cross that boundary as a registered callback or an out-parameter, never a direct call into SCSI code. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, 2-node TCP rig 2026-09-17, build E927E501A55C222725566A8, tests/evidence/sess41_d0381/armA_FIXED_E927E501.log: after an out-of-band release of the reservation, the stand-in node's repair landed at t+62 s, of which only the last 20.50 s was its deliberate takeover deadline. The other ~42 s was purely waiting for its own 60 s audit to come round, while the target had already raised a UA it could have acted on at once. With the repair-authority half fixed in 0.86.2, detection latency is now the dominant term in how long an MXFS cluster stays unfenceable after a reservation loss.
defects.next: DESIGN CONSULT ALREADY HELD (Astra, 2026-09-17); its hazards must be answered before coding, not after. (1) A UA is PENDING SENSE, not a push: nothing is delivered until some command exposes it, so instrumenting only the PR wrappers may not help an idle node AT ALL -- an auditor's next PR command is the very audit the trigger was meant to accelerate. MEASURE FIRST where a UA is actually observed, including whether the SCSI midlayer consumes and retries it on ordinary data I/O before MXFS ever sees it. (2) Do not treat all of ASC 2Ah as the PR-relevant class (it carries unrelated changes), but do not whitelist exact codes only either -- a coarse or vendor-specific code for the same event would be silently uncovered. Preferred: definite PR/reset codes take a fast lane; an unrecognised UA invalidates the cached state and schedules a coalesced, bounded check, with counters and rate-limited diagnostics. (3) 2Ah/05h REGISTRATIONS PREEMPTED is evidence about the OBSERVING nexus's own registration and belongs in the existing fenced-self inspection path, not the ordinary auditor delay; receiving it is not the same as a completed inspection. (4) Separate the two actions: logical cache invalidation must be IMMEDIATE at notification time, or a fencing path can consume the stale snapshot meanwhile, while target interrogation stays asynchronous (a synchronous PRIN from a heartbeat or data-path thread is the wrong default). Guard the race where a check already in flight clears a dirty flag set after it started -- use a sequence number, not a boolean, and account for the check's OWN UA retry generating the callback. (5) A PR-relevant UA met INSIDE a PREEMPT or PREEMPT-AND-ABORT retry loop must not be transparently retried: it may mean the assumptions established before the fence began are now stale, so return revalidate/restart rather than hiding it. (6) At 32 nodes jitter alone is insufficient -- coalesce a burst into ONE pending obligation whose deadline later events may advance but never push out, rate-limit executions with at most one check in flight per LU, and keep UNKNOWN as UNKNOWN rather than letting backoff turn it into a stale OK. (7) A reset UA (29h) does NOT imply lost registrations: PRs are meant to survive resets distinct from power loss, so it must never clear software registration state or trigger a REGISTER. TESTS the consult says this patch must pass, beyond re-running the two existing arms in tests/resv_health_detect.sh and tests/resv_selfgone_withdraw.sh: idle victim, with time-to-first-UA-observation measured SEPARATELY from observation-to-inspection; a UA consumed on ordinary I/O, proving whether the callback sees it at all; a notification arriving during a successful check, proving it is not cleared by that check; a UA storm, proving a bounded command rate and no deadline starvation; total PR loss, proving the maintainer does not automatically REGISTER itself; and a reset with PR retained, proving no false withdrawal. RELATED: the repair-authority half of this area was fixed and verified in 0.86.2 -- a stand-in now takes the repair over when the elected maintainer is gone -- and this record is ONLY the event-driven trigger.
defects.impact_why: Pace of fencing repair: after an out-of-band reservation release the stand-in's repair landed at t+62 s, about 42 s of it waiting for the 60 s audit (tests/evidence/sess41_d0381/armA_FIXED_E927E501.log); the reservation was repaired, nothing corrupted, hung or shut down. A data effect needs a second independent fault (a peer death whose zombie I/O lands) inside that window, which the record does not show; it stays in the queue as a fencing-latency defect.

defects.summary: Two nodes alternating aligned 4 KiB O_DIRECT writes into one shared file with a 20000-extent, two-level extent tree (about 97 bmbt blocks) complete about 425 writes per node in 90 s (4.7 writes/s each), against about 15000 per node in 90 s on a 16-block file under the same contention; and a buffered read (cat) of that 4 GiB sparse file on one node while the peer writes into it does not finish inside 90 s. Every grant handoff on a btree-format file re-reads the tree cold: the reload evicts every cached bmbt block the inode owns (P59-BMBT-EVICT, bmbt_evict=1000 capped per lap) and the next extent load re-reads all of them (iomap_iread_pr 425-528 per lap), so the cost of a handoff grows with the tree, not with the write.
defects.evidence: tests/dio_write_conversion_deadlock.sh on build 8E4C6A2CC5EAC566F5438FD (0.87.5), 2/tcp: NOCAT=1 EXTEND=1 EXTSPAN=1048576 PREFILL=20000 90 s lap (tests/evidence/20260918T041101Z_dwcd_fin_hugenc) test1 'WRITER ok=428 failed=0', test2 'ok=425 failed=0', iomap_iread_pr=425 on each, bmbt_evict=1000 (cap) on each, rel_bmbt_flushed 1/3; the same lap with the preamble read (20260918T040220Z_dwcd_fin_huge): test1 'WRITER ok=0 failed=0' because its cat of the 4 GiB file ran the whole 90 s window (iomap_iread_pr=528) while test2 wrote 2749; the 65536-block span lap (035930Z_dwcd_fin_deep) likewise test1 ok=0 (cat, iomap_iread_pr=736), test2 4567. The 16-block aligned lap on the same build: 14818/14999 writes in 90 s.
defects.next: Measure what one handoff of the 97-block tree costs, stage by stage (reload eviction walk, extent load reads, release scan) with the per-release timing line, and compare with a handoff that keeps the cached blocks that a peer did not change (a per-block generation or a release-time list of blocks this tenure wrote, so the reload evicts only what changed). A buffered reader should not have to re-acquire per mapping while a writer extends the file: consider a PR tenure that survives a peer's EX for the read window, or readahead that maps in larger chunks under one grant.
defects.impact_why: pace only: no write failed, no image differed, nothing hung past the lap; the 2/tcp release bar excludes pace

defects.summary: A node that unmounts cleanly and remounts in the same boot (the same derived PR key) while its peer is also mounting is fenced by that peer: the predecessor's heartbeat slot is released RETIRE_PENDING at put_super and umount returns, the successor re-registers the identical key 2.4 s later and takes over the PR-ledger entry, but its own settlement of the predecessor's record (P305-RETIRE-SETTLED-OWN) lands only 8.6 s after the release, behind register, reserve and the FENCECAP probe; the peer's mount thread sighted the record 0.1 s after the release, held its admission (P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD rc=1 WAITING) and at 9.7 s, its 10 s mount grace spent, preempt-and-aborted the key, naming the successor (P-PR-FENCE dead node 3432382203, P-VERGATE-FENCE slot=0 state=4). The successor's mount is refused (rc=32) and the predecessor's deferred release, unregistering 12 s after the slot release, finds the key gone and its ledger RETIRED write answered RESERVATION CONFLICT (P-PRKEY-RETIRED rc=-52). The unregister itself did not conflict; the conflict on the ledger write is the consequence of the peer's preempt. This is the s49ctl hazard the 0.87.11 mount-thread grace was designed to cover (a successor settles EMPTY within a second); measured, the successor's settle takes 8.6 s against a 10 s grace.
defects.evidence: tests/d0965_remount_bracket_race.sh healthy lap s58h-H22 on 0.87.19, tests/evidence/20260918T232955Z_d0965race_s58h-H22-d0965_remount_bracket_race-ok. test1 (A then A', lap1_test1.txt): 3251.887 P304-RETIRE-QUIESCED at=put_super submitted=6534; 3251.915 P304-RETIRE-PENDING-RELEASED slot 0; 3252.795 A' PREOBSERVE (mount start, 0.9 s after the release); 3254.355 P-PRKEY-REGISTERED key=0x702f116e501f9c5e keys=2 and P305-PR-SAME-BOOT-RETIRE-PENDING slot=0 node=3079361979; 3254.384 ledger idx=0 REGISTERED node=3432382203 (the successor took the entry); 3255.9-3257.4 P303-FENCECAP/OK; 3260.500 P305-RETIRE-SETTLED-OWN slot=0 proof=own-registration-bracket, P305-RETIRE-SETTLED 'mount proceeds' (8.6 s after the release); 3263.905 the old incarnation's deferred release unregisters (P-PR-DEPARTURE-UNHELD op=unregister, 12.0 s after the release); 3263.923 'sd 3:0:0:0: reservation conflict' then P-PRKEY-RETIRED idx=0 node=3432382203 rc=-52; lap1_amount.txt: mount rc=32 wall_ms=11188, P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD slot=0 rc=1. test2 (B', lap1_test2.txt, win_grace_6_test2.txt): 173.463 PREOBSERVE (its own mount start); 173.539 P274-CLAIM-RETIRE-PENDING-SKIP slot=0 node=3079361979 (first sight, <=0.1 s after A's release by the clock offset the release/sighting pair fixes); 174.948 P304-RETIRE-PENDING-SEEN slot=0 state=UNKNOWN; 174.990 P304-RETIRE-WORKER result=PRESENT (the successor's identical key); 175.240 P304-RETIRE-PRESENT-GRACE seen=290 ms ago and P-ADMIT-RETIRE-PENDING-HELD slot=0 rc=1; 183.224 P-PR-FENCE preempt-and-aborted dead node 3432382203 (key 0x702f116e501f9c5e) gen=4464 EXCLUSION PROVED, P236-FENCEKIND kind=PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE(16), P-VERGATE-FENCE slot=0 node=3432382203 epoch=12367608096848124051 state=4 pr_fence=ok (9.7 s after first sight; MXFS_DISKLOCK_RETIRE_MOUNT_GRACE_MS=10000, dlm/disklock.h:128); BMOUNT rc=0 wall_ms=8864. Code: the successor's own settle is v5_p305_settle_retire_pending (dlm/v5_mount.c:3235, own-key arm 3268-3286) called from the mount at 14176/14652 after the PR context and the disklock exist; the predecessor's unregister is in the deferred release (v5_mount.c:15751, inside mxfs_v5_dlm_shutdown_defer_release at 15408) after peer shutdown, DLM destroy and the tauth ledger close, which is why it trails the slot release by 12 s. The same harness passed s57b-11 (0.87.19, tests/evidence/laps_s57/): the race has a ~1 s margin and does not always lose.
defects.next: 1. DESIGN CONSULT before any change (fencing semantics, hard to reverse): the successor re-registers the identical per-boot key before it can settle the predecessor's RETIRE_PENDING record, so for the whole register-to-settle window (measured 6.1 s: 3254.4 to 3260.5) the record reads PRESENT to every peer and the peer's grace is the only thing standing between the successor and a preempt of its live key. Shapes to bring: (a) settle the own-boot record BEFORE re-registering the key, when READ KEYS can prove the key ABSENT (the predecessor's deferred release must then unregister before umount returns, or the successor must wait for it: mxfs_v5_dlm_departure_lock already serializes 'same-boot re-registration against the old unmount's late phase'); (b) move the own-settle ahead of the FENCECAP probe so the window shrinks to the register itself; (c) a peer whose sync lookup finds the key PRESENT with the same host+boot identity as the record and a ledger entry already REGISTERED to a NEWER node id treats it as a successor in progress and extends its grace rather than withdrawing. 2. Reproduce on demand: tests/d0965_remount_bracket_race.sh test1 test2 3 <label>, and stamp the successor's register-to-settle window (P-PRKEY-REGISTERED to P305-RETIRE-SETTLED-OWN) and the peer's first-sight-to-fence window on every lap. 3. Fix at the proven cause, then three laps with the successor never fenced and the predecessor's ledger RETIRED write rc=0.
defects.impact_why: Availability, not integrity or stability: the predecessor quiesced and released before the successor existed (P304-RETIRE-QUIESCED submitted=6534, then the slot release), the successor was fenced at admission before it went writable (its mount refused rc=32, no I/O of its own in flight), the peer mounted (rc=0) and nothing crashed, hung or shut down on either node in the lap. What it costs is a same-boot remount that races a peer's mount; it stays in the queue as a fencing-design defect (a live successor fenced on its predecessor's record).

defects.summary: A live foreign-generation heartbeat writer on the shared LUN is invisible to MXFS and its slot is claimable: hb_gen_foreign classes any ACTIVE record whose fs_gen is not ours as a pre-mkfs ghost with no liveness test, the join gate and heartbeat monitor skip it with no log line, and mxfs_disklock_claim_slot treats it as claimable, so a host still running an old mxfs on the same LUN heartbeats (and, whenever the LUN is unreserved, writes its stale filesystem) into a live cluster's platter with nothing in any node's journal naming it.
defects.evidence: Measured s67 (2/tcp, QNAP LUN naa.6e843b6393a5a6ed918bd4f4fdb8e7d6): with both rig VMs torn down (mxfs unloaded), slot 2 carried an ACTIVE record node=1216714748 fs_gen=0 epoch=0 pr_key=0 whose ts_ms advanced 2016 ms per dump interval (tests/evidence/20260919T134608Z_foreign_writer_serv_s67/). The writer was serv.localdomain 192.168.1.5: Debian 5.10.0-45, the physical-campaign DKMS mxfs.ko (2026-05), /etc/fstab _netdev mount of /dev/sdb at every boot, mounted 2026-09-17T18:46 CDT, 48027 mxfs kernel lines since. Its writes are fenced only by the cluster's SCSI reservation: a scratch WE-AR reservation from test1 froze the stamp for 6 s and the clear released it, and serv's journal shows 'heartbeat write failed: -52' bursts exactly in the reservation windows. In every unreserved window (mkfs, the gap before the first mount reserves, PR transitions) its heartbeat and its stale filesystem's writes land: the s62e mkfs zero_region verify FAIL ('K' of MXLK at the slot 2 sector) was this writer, misattributed for three sessions to 'a node from the previous lap'. Code: dlm/disklock.c hb_gen_foreign (line ~236) has no liveness term; the join gate at ~5434 and the claim loop at ~11440 skip/claim on that test alone; no P-line names a foreign-generation ACTIVE record. The rig-side fix (prep refuses under any advancing record, 0.89.4) closes the mkfs hole only; the module still admits a mount beside a live foreign writer silently.
defects.next: Design the liveness term with a consult: a foreign-generation ACTIVE record whose timestamp advances across the heartbeat interval is a LIVE FOREIGN WRITER, not a ghost — log it (slot, node, fs_gen, stamp delta) at the join gate and in the monitor, never claim its slot, and decide whether admission must refuse (the writer shares the platter; the reservation fences it during tenure but not across PR transitions) or proceed with the slot excluded. Prove with an injected writer: a second initiator stamping a foreign-gen record on a spare slot while the fleet mounts; assert the P-line, the slot skip, and the admission decision; then a claim attempt on that slot under a cleared reservation to show the collision the fix prevents.
defects.impact_why: It corrupts nothing and hangs nothing under the release configuration as measured: the cluster's WE-AR reservation blocks the foreign initiator's writes for the whole tenure (stamp frozen under a scratch reservation, EBADE bursts in serv's journal), and the rig-side guard now refuses to format under it. The exposure is the unreserved windows and the missing diagnostic, so it stays in the queue below the release bar.

defects.summary: The mount-time orphan sweep runs before the mount's recovery census and the join gate's declarations, so reclamation of departed authorities is attempted while this node has not yet reconstructed the platter's recovery obligations; the 0.89.4 platter-backed retention predicate closes the measured hole, but the ordering itself was ruled wrong: destructive maintenance should follow an inventory of ACTIVE occupancy and victim-to-obligation index, and the ACTIVE -> RECOVERY_GUARD -> released handoff should be stated and tested as an invariant with no durable gap.
defects.evidence: Design consult Astra 2026-09-19 on D-A-MOUNT-S-ORPHAN-SWEEP-RETIRES-THE-LEDGER-RECORDS (fixed at 0.89.4 by the platter-backed predicate, measured s67h/s67k): the consult's shape beyond the shipped change — (A) inventory before destructive maintenance: fs generation, read and validate the table, populate ACTIVE occupancy and a separate victim-to-obligation index, discover guards regardless of owner/lease/marker, schedule adoption of stranded attempts; (B) run the opportunistic sweep after that census and the join gate's classification, never before; (C) one retention rule at every destructive choke point immediately before the action; (D) release only by the recovery state machine's durable completion, never by age or owner change. Code: dlm/v5_mount.c v5_orphan_sweep_queue at mount (~14491) runs before the barrier's declarations; dlm/dlm.c dlm_orphan_scan dead test = occupant map + view. No failure measured after the 0.89.4 predicate (d0356 s67k, d0981 s67i, sole_survivor s67j, join_during_takeover s67m all PASS).
defects.next: Move the mount-time sweep behind the mount's recovery census (after the barrier's declarations and the stranded-attempt adoption), make the census seed the pending markers, and prove the sweep's ordering with the d0356 shape run with the sweep deliberately exercised before local declarations; state the ACTIVE->GUARD->released invariant in docs/tcp-authority-ledger.md and add the crash points around that handoff to the fence crash matrix.
defects.impact_why: Nothing measured fails after the 0.89.4 predicate: the retention rule at the choke point protects the records whatever the sweep's ordering. The ordering is a design hazard the consult named, not an observed corruption, hang or crash.

defects.summary: COMPARE AND WRITE is submitted to the SCSI midlayer with a retry allowance, so a CAW that already executed can be re-issued after error handling and then MISCOMPARE against the data it itself wrote - reporting a FALSE FAILURE for a compare-and-swap that in fact committed. Every disklock CAS in the tree rides this primitive.
defects.evidence: ESTABLISHED BY CODE INSPECTION, not yet measured. pal/linux/kern.c mxfs_pal_bdev_compare_and_write issues opcode 0x89 through scsi_execute_cmd(..., 30 * HZ, 1, &args); the penultimate argument is the midlayer RETRY COUNT, so the block layer may re-issue the CDB once on its own after error handling has aborted it, and the caller sees only one return value. COMPARE AND WRITE is not idempotent in the way a retry assumes: if the first execution applied the write and its response was lost or timed out, the re-issued command compares the caller's ORIGINAL expected image against the NEW on-platter contents, miscompares, and returns failure for an operation that succeeded. Found while auditing the same parameter on the PREEMPT AND ABORT wrapper for D-FENCE-POSTSUBMIT-AMBIGUITY-NO-RECONCILIATION-381, where the design consult's requirement is that 'no queued retry, retransmission, reinstatement or error-handling path can generate another execution-capable instance of the operation'. Every other passthrough in that file also carries retries=1; the reads and the FUA WRITE(16) are idempotent and unaffected. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which callers a false-negative CAS actually harms. The disklock protocol generally re-reads after a failed CAS, and the certificate-publication path was explicitly taught at 0.89.13 to treat a failed CAS as an UNKNOWN commit outcome, so some callers already tolerate it; the slot-claim, heartbeat and recovery-descriptor paths have not been audited against it.
defects.next: 1) Decide the retry count deliberately per command class rather than uniformly: a non-idempotent state-changing command needs retries=0 so that exactly one execution attempt happens per call and a lost response stays honestly UNKNOWN. 2) Before changing it, audit every caller of mxfs_pal_bdev_compare_and_write for what a FALSE FAILURE does - a caller that re-reads and reconciles is safe, a caller that treats failure as 'my write did not happen' is not, and that is the list this record needs. 3) Measure it rather than reasoning about it: the initiator-side shape is to correlate the passthrough and error-handler events with the target's command traffic, which does not need target instrumentation. 4) Do NOT fix this in the same change as the PREEMPT AND ABORT retry count - they are different commands with different callers and a shared patch makes neither result attributable. ===== CALLER AUDIT DONE (0.90.129 tree, read in full by a subagent, the premises re-read in the parent): (1) THE DEFAULT PATH IS NOT RE-SENT. caw_path defaults to 1 (pal/linux/kern.c 'static int mxfs_caw_path = 1'), caw_manual_bio sets scmd->allowed = 0 (sreq->retries = 0 on RHEL 9), so a command libiscsi fails with DID_TRANSPORT_DISRUPTED at iscsi_conn_stop (libiscsi.c fail_scsi_tasks) goes to maybe_retry (scsi_error.c) and is NOT retried (++retries <= allowed fails); the in-driver resubmit (goto caw_submit) is only on CHECK CONDITION UNIT ATTENTION, which a target reports instead of executing the command. caw_verify defaults to 0, so the post-CAS verify read that returns -EAGAIN on a peer overwrite does not run either. So on the defaults a CAW that landed cannot come back -EAGAIN; its only ambiguous outcome is -EIO (answer lost). retries=1 remains ONLY on caw_path=0 (scsi_execute_cmd/scsi_execute ... 30*HZ, 1) and the false -EAGAIN ONLY with caw_verify=1 (peer CAS between our CAS and the verify read). (2) -EIO ON A LANDED CAW, default path: dlm_caw caw_slot_amb sets answer_lost and its internal retry re-reads and resolves (returns 0 when the slot equals our write image, caw_answer_lost_resolve=1 default) - SAFE. Elsewhere -EIO arms fail closed with liveness costs only: prledger publish -> mount refused (a same-boot remount reuses the entry); bootstrap claim/reseal -> record left CLAIMED with our identity until a same-boot resume or fence-takeover; disklock claim_slot -> falls to claim_slot_noncaw, whose FUA pass matches our record, then P311 refuses the mount; guard_slot/guard_refresh -> guard stranded ~62 s; release_slot -> PR key kept, peers expire to WITHDRAWN and fence a clean slice; tauth ticket -> poison+reconcile. No integrity loss found on -EIO. (3) UNDER THE NON-DEFAULT KNOBS (false -EAGAIN), UNSAFE: dlm_caw unlock (:11534-11563 continue -> re-read NL -> RELEASED without clr_committed, so lreq_clr_end runs with false and a concurrent local shortcut acquire can publish a grant on a cleared holder bit) and convert-downgrade via caw_slot_clearing (lreq_clr_end gets caw_may_have_written(-EAGAIN)=false); prledger publish (-EAGAIN -> idx++, a second REGISTERED entry for one key); claim_slot (fresh claim redone as own-stamp reclaim, slice_adopted wrong). UNCERTAIN: lock acquire's 'Already hold it' arm (:9543) does not track_held, so a grant that landed under a false -EAGAIN is not in ctx->held for release_all. Not read: ~25 other caw_slot callers, recov_cas_durable callers :7331 :8040 :8473 :9358 :9450 :10122. NEXT, one change each: (a) caw_path=0 retries 1 -> 0 (makes path 0 match the default; the dlm_caw resolver then handles the -EIO); (b) caw_verify mismatch returns -EIO (outcome unknown) instead of -EAGAIN, so callers take their answer-lost arm; (c) the -EIO liveness arms above (bootstrap claim, claim_slot noncaw fallback refusing a mount whose CAW record is on disk). ===== (a) AND (b) ARE IN THE 0.90.129 TREE (pal/linux/kern.c, CHANGELOG 0.90.129 'A lock swap ... that landed is never reported as one that did not'): the caw_path knob and its scsi_execute_cmd path are removed, so every CAW goes out once through caw_manual_bio (scmd->allowed = 0; the only reissue is on UNIT ATTENTION); caw_verify=1 mismatch returns -EIO (outcome unknown) instead of -EAGAIN. That removes every false -EAGAIN found by the caller audit. STILL OPEN, why the record stays: (c) the -EIO liveness arms (bootstrap claim left CLAIMED until a same-boot resume or fence-takeover; claim_slot's noncaw fallback refusing a mount whose CAW record landed, P311; guard stranded ~62 s; prledger publish refusing the mount), and the callers the audit did not read (~25 other caw_slot callers; recov_cas_durable callers). Next: read those callers for an arm that treats -EIO as 'my write did not happen'; then measure an -EIO on a landed CAW (an answer dropped after the target executed it) at a slot claim, and confirm the mount does not strand.
defects.impact_why: DOES NOT CROSS THE 2-NODE TCP RELEASE BAR, and the earlier integrity classification was a fail-closed guess made when this was filed, not a measurement. What the code establishes: recov_cas_durable (dlm/disklock.c) returns the CAS failure and the caller RE-READS the descriptor and re-decides from the platter - its own comment states the contract, 'the recovery stays at its current stage (fail closed) and the caller re-decides'. Every disklock CAS is a read-modify-CAS loop over durable state, so a false-negative costs a retry, not correctness: the re-read sees whatever actually landed, including our own image. That is the same shape 0.89.13 formalised deliberately for the certificate path, where a failed CAS is treated as an UNKNOWN commit outcome. No path is known that turns a false negative into lost or corrupted data, and none that hangs or crashes a node. NOT DISPROVED, and it stays in the queue: the slot-claim callers (disklock.c:11496, :12750) have not been audited, and a node that believes it failed to claim a slot it in fact holds could strand that record. That audit is what this record is open for - it is not a release gate.

defects.summary: A durable fence certificate of a class this build has revoked makes the filesystem unmountable on every node, and no operator route to dispose of the record is finished: chk_mxfs --accept-quarantine-loss implements steps 1-4 of its ruling and deliberately stops before the destructive ones.
defects.evidence: MEASURED 2026-09-20 on the 2-node TCP rig, build 36FCAFE109AFE7F324BE343, eight arms of tests/fence_kind_matrix.sh (tests/evidence/20260920T113047Z_fkm_s84b_retired16 and seven siblings, each fails=0). A recovery-descriptor certificate of kind 16, 19, 20, 21 or an unknown kind is forged into an unused heartbeat slot by tools/recov_forge with its crc and identity binding recomputed - the shape an older build left on the platter. The mounting node then refuses the claim by class (P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED naming the revoked class verbatim), replays nothing, and the mount ABORTS with rc=32 at 123-124 s. That refusal is CORRECT and is the fix this version shipped; the defect is what happens next. Every subsequent mount of that filesystem, on every node, does the same thing, because the record is durable and nothing removes it. The bound is the mount barrier's own: it prints P-BARRIER-GHOST-EXTEND undeclared=1 window_ms=62000 bound_ms=122000, since a guard slot with no live heartbeat is an undeclared death and buys the one-time extension. THE DISPOSAL ROUTE IS INCOMPLETE, established by reading tools/chk_mxfs.c: do_accept_quarantine_loss's own header states 'THIS BUILD IMPLEMENTS STEPS 1-4 AND STOPS THERE, deliberately' - validate the verdict, take exclusive maintenance ownership, refuse if any non-quarantined slice is dirty, archive off-volume. Steps 5-9 (record LOSS_ACCEPTED, reinitialise the slice, consistency repair, CHECK_COMPLETE, clear the source slot) are unwritten, so the sector is never cleared. It also keys on a QUARANTINED outcome record; a revoked certificate is a live FENCED descriptor with no outcome record at all, so the command does not address this shape even once its remaining steps land.
defects.next: Two separable pieces. (1) THE SHAPE: decide whether a revoked-class certificate is reachable by the same operator route as a quarantined slice, or needs its own. The design ruling docs/rulings/fence-certificate-proof-profiles-and-legacy-revocation.md is explicit that availability does not supply the missing evidence - 'a stranded pending recovery has two options: obtain a new, independently supported proof and issue a new certificate, or stay blocked' - so the route must be an explicit, confirmed ACCEPTANCE OF LOSS, never a relabelling of the certificate and never a silent clear. The forged matrix already proves the refusing path does not rewrite what it refused, which is the invariant any disposal route must not break. (2) THE STEPS: finish chk_mxfs steps 5-9 under the sess377 ruling's ordering, or state in the operator documentation that the only route today is mkfs and that the archive step exists to make that survivable. Do not close this by noting that the refusal is correct: the refusal being correct is why this record exists.
defects.impact_why: Availability, not integrity or stability. Nothing is corrupted - the whole point is that the replay is refused - and nothing hangs or crashes: the mount returns rc=32 at 123-124 s, inside the 122 s bound the barrier prints for itself, and the survivor served throughout every arm (measured, tests/evidence/20260920T113047Z_fkm_s84b_retired16 and seven siblings). What is lost is the ability to mount a filesystem that carries such a record, on every node, permanently. Under the 2-node TCP release bar - 100% data integrity and stability - that does not gate the release. It is in the queue because a fleet upgrading from 0.89.12-0.89.15 with a certificate already on the platter is exactly the population this class of record was retired for.

Native XFS makes thousands per second on the same hardware, so this is far past the 2x-native ceiling.

Then profile one node's private-dir create loop (the per-create phases: dialloc/CAW inode reservation, the grant on the new inode, the directory's grant, log force) to find where ~29 ms per create goes; the related shared-directory records attribute most blocked time to the CAW inode-grant wait.

defects.summary: Deleting 500 small files on one node that the other node created took 30.4 s on the 2/tcp Proxmox pair (pve9-2 deleting pve9-1's files), ~16 unlinks/s. Native XFS removes 500 files in well under a second, so this is far past 2x native.
defects.evidence: tests/evidence/pve9_release_0.89.80/del_f_138.log ('real 0m30.444s', del_rc=0), tests/evidence/pve9_release_0.89.80/create_f_194.log (500 created on pve9-1), tests/evidence/pve9_release_0.89.80/count_194.log (0 after the remote delete). 0.89.80, PVE 9 kernel 6.17.2-1-pve, QNAP LUN over in-guest iSCSI.

Still far past 2x native.

defects.summary: A node that crashes mid-unmount after its peer has unmounted cleanly takes 130-145 s to mount again, spent in the whole-cluster bootstrap's two ~64 s frozen-table observation windows (P-BOOT-SCAN-FROZEN) before it may declare the total outage and fence its previous incarnation; when both nodes mount at once, the one that loses the bootstrap claim is refused after ~68 s with EBUSY (P-BOOT-MOUNT-REFUSED rc=-16), which mount(8) reports as 'Transport endpoint is not connected'.
defects.evidence: tests/crash_mid_umount_remount.sh on 0.89.85 (srcversion C46F4EF317B7E80B3DDAE03), test1/test2, QNAP LUN (wwn-0x6e843b6393a5a6ed918bd4f4fdb8e7d6), 500 files written and synced on the victim, peer unmounted cleanly, victim destroyed 1 s into its unmount. ARM=alone (tests/evidence/crash_mid_umount_remount/alone_20260924T114811): victim's mount 143153 ms; P306 LU-reset fence admitted at 156.2 s uptime, certified 157.3 s, foreign replay of 502 manifest entries, P-BOOT-RECOVERY-COMPLETE 163.3 s; peer then mounted in 7215 ms. ARM=together (together_20260924T115312): peer became bootstrap owner and completed recovery (138740 ms); victim refused, P-BOOT-MOUNT-REFUSED rc=-16 at 87.4 s, mount(2) 'Transport endpoint is not connected'. Both arms: platter before recovery 504 allocated inodes, after 504, chk_mxfs clean, all 500 files visible from the peer. The 0.89.84 first sighting (packaged_round ubuntu2404_0.89.84_20260924T094458) was the same shape, confounded by the mount being issued while the node booted. Two earlier runs of the reproducer read the wrong LUN (/dev/sda, the LIO bench target) and are void.
defects.next: Reproduce without the lease bug: crash one node of a mounted 2-node TCP pair mid-unmount (sysrq-c on the guest during umount), remount it with peer= while the peer also mounts, and time each phase from dmesg: fence admission, certification, replay start, mxfs_slice_stabilize exit, mount return. Read what mxfs_slice_stabilize waits for and what satisfies it when the only other node is itself mounting. ===== Correction after reading xfs/xfs_log_recover.c:298: the mount task's msleep inside mxfs_slice_stabilize, captured 0-4 s after 'foreign replay of dead slot 0' began, is the designed stability proof (mxfs_fr_stab_passes=2 re-reads, mxfs_fr_stab_interval_ms=2000, deadline 45 s), not evidence of a stall. The measured delay is the fence admission: the victim's own key was already absent and the peer was registered, so no LU-reset fence could be admitted until the peer's mount gave up. The reproduction must mount the crashed node only after it has finished booting, and must separate 'peer idle and mounted', 'peer unmounted' and 'peer mounting concurrently'. ===== Two separate fixes: the frozen-table window length (why two ~64 s windows when the only other node is known to have departed cleanly — its GOODBYE/clean slot release is on disk), and mapping P-BOOT-MOUNT-REFUSED to an errno and message that tell the operator to retry once the bootstrap owner finishes.
defects.impact_why: Measured in both arms: no data lost (504/504 inodes, 500/500 files, chk_mxfs clean before and after recovery), no node crashed, hung or shut down; every mount returned, the slow one completing recovery and the refused one returning EBUSY. What remains is mount pace after a total outage and a misleading refusal errno.

defects.summary: tests/suite/fio_perf.sh takes 104-112 s of its 120 s budget on 2/tcp, so an ordinary rise in host load exhausts it: the 0.89.86 suite run failed it BUDGET_EXHAUSTED on both nodes.
defects.evidence: 2/tcp, test1/test2, QNAP LUN. 0.89.85 suite (C46F4EF317B7E80B3DDAE03): PASS 107s/120s, seqW=102MiB/s seqR=173MiB/s randW=28832iops randR=30515iops, hostload 8.57. 0.89.86 suite (67FB1FBF8A0DED66E87731F, tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_0.89.86.log): FAIL nodes_pass=0/2 states:BUDGET_EXHAUSTED=2 hostload=8.27. Same build rerun twice (tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_0.89.86_fio_rerun{1,2}.log): PASS 112s/120s (seqW=109 seqR=142 randW=28809 randR=31137, hostload 25.73) and PASS 104s/120s (seqW=111 seqR=112 randW=26954 randR=32574, hostload 24.99). Throughput is the same across builds; only the wall's margin is thin. The 0.89.86 change (the owned-metadata gate) touches unpublished-inode grants, which a fio job on existing files does not reach. 0.89.88 suite (4F12CE2378A09CD0A647E46, tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_0.89.88.log): FAIL BUDGET_EXHAUSTED=2 hostload=10.06, the other 29 tests PASS. Same build after a fresh prep, rerun twice (tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_0.89.88_fio_rerun{1,2}.log): PASS 105s/120s (seqW=111 seqR=192 randW=26652 randR=23641, hostload 20.12) and PASS 104s/120s (seqW=112 seqR=125 randW=27454 randR=25405, hostload 12.41) - the same margin and throughput as 0.89.86.
defects.next: Find where the 104-112 s goes before touching the budget, which must not be widened: read fio_perf.sh's job list and per-phase timing (fixed-runtime jobs vs fixed-size), time each phase on one run, and compare the fixed-size phases against native XFS on the same LUN with fio_perf_vs_xfs's numbers. If the jobs are time-based, the budget's derivation is what is wrong and must be re-derived from the jobs' runtimes; if they are size-based, the slow phase is the defect. ===== 2026-10-18 (session 87) WHERE THE 104-112 s WENT, FROM THE RECORD'S OWN NUMBERS AND THE BASELINES (miner sweep of data/criteria.json, tests/evidence and the .xfs_fio_baseline files). The jobs are size-based (tests/suite/fio_perf.sh: --size, no --runtime). Per node at N=2 SIZE is 1024m (2048/N clamped to [64,1024]) and RSIZE 64m; at N=1 SIZE is also 1024m (2048 clamped), so a 2-node run moves TWICE the native single-node run's bytes through the one target. The record's runs were on the QNAP LUN over gigabit iSCSI: MXFS's 2-node aggregate there was seqW 102-112 MiB/s, seqR 112-192 MiB/s, randW 26652-28832, randR 23641-32574 iops (the record's evidence), and native XFS on the same QNAP LUN read seqW 108, seqR 111 MiB/s, randW 18714, randR 26214 iops (.xfs_fio_baseline.net-mesh-direct.qnap.json, 2026-09-05): MXFS ran at the target's line rate, i.e. at native throughput, and the wall is the volume over that rate. The 120 s budget's derivation (tests/criteria/TIMEOUT_BUDGETS.md:189 'LUN ~2GB/s => ~60-90s steady-state') assumed a 2 GB/s LUN, so on a ~110 MiB/s target it sat below 2x native for the same bytes. The QNAP rig is retired (tools/mxfs_rig_tag.sh:29-31; 16 of 17 cluster markers rig scst-fio); on the pooled SCST LUNs every 2-node TCP fio_perf record in data/criteria.json is PASS: 2/net/mesh/direct 11/11 at 30-55 s (median 40), 2/net/mesh/mpath 9/9 at 36-54 s (median 43), against native 1/xfs 27-32 s (median 28) on the same pool, all within 2x. PROPOSED DISPOSITION: DISPROVED (direct evidence that the measured wall was the target's bandwidth at native XFS throughput, not an MXFS slowness); before removing, re-read the record's evidence lines and the qnap baseline file by hand, and check data/criteria.pvephys.json's 2/net/mesh/drbd fio_perf BUDGET_EXHAUSTED laps (2026-10-14, physical pair) against native XFS-on-DRBD for the same bytes: those are a different rig and need their own reading (their native baseline file .xfs_fio_baseline.net-mesh-drbd.pvephys is root 0600). ===== 2026-10-18 (session 94) ONE OF THE TWO PRE-REMOVAL CHECKS DONE. The physical pair's 2/net/mesh/drbd fio_perf laps (data/criteria.pvephys.json): 2026-10-14T17:45:40Z BUDGET_EXHAUSTED both nodes at 116 s, 18:14:55Z FAIL elapsed 133 s > 120 s (functional checks passed), then PASS 18:46:12Z and 2026-10-15T00:50:09Z (137 s, status PASS). The failing lap's MXFS two-node aggregate seqW 212 MiB/s, seqR 747 MiB/s, randW 22518, randR 148632 iops against native XFS-on-DRBD on the same pair (.xfs_fio_baseline.net-mesh-drbd.pvephys.json, root 0600, read with sudo) seqW 101, seqR 222 MiB/s, randW 17237, randR 51848 iops at size 1024m: MXFS moved each phase's bytes at or above native throughput, and the job (tests/suite/fio_perf.sh: size-based, SIZE per node, FIO_PASSES=4 measured passes) moves twice native's bytes at N=2, so those walls are the DRBD target's bandwidth, not MXFS slowness. The QNAP baseline file (.xfs_fio_baseline.net-mesh-direct.qnap.json) reads seqW 108, seqR 111 MiB/s, randW 18714, randR 26214 iops, as quoted above. STILL OWED before removal: re-read the record's own fio_perf lines by hand; a grep for 'fio_perf' in tests/evidence/suite_2tcp_0.89.86.log, _fio_rerun1/2.log, suite_2tcp_0.89.88.log and its reruns found no line, so locate where those suite runs wrote their fio_perf rows (the logs' own format) before the --why cites them. ===== 2026-10-19 (session 122) the suite logs the evidence cites (suite_2tcp_0.89.86.log, its _fio_rerun1/2, suite_2tcp_0.89.88.log and its reruns) are in none of ~/src/mxfs/tests/evidence, /src/mxfs/tests/evidence or any ~/src/mxfs-*/tests/evidence (ls by name). NEXT: look for the same runs' fio_perf rows in data/criteria.json by srcversion (67FB1FBF8A0DED66E87731F, 4F12CE2378A09CD0A647E46, C46F4EF317B7E80B3DDAE03; a recursive grep of both evidence trees for them overran 120 s and was stopped), else cite the board records the session-87 entry already read.
defects.impact_why: Pace only: in every run, failed or passed, fio completed its I/O on both nodes, the suite continued, and no node crashed, hung, shut down or logged a BUG/Oops; no data check failed.

defects.summary: After a peer is declared dead, fenced and replayed, and the frozen victim resumes (its retired identity's reconnects refused, P164-DEAD-REJECT), a file create on the survivor stalled about 60 s: tests/selinux_svirt_mxfs.sh's qemu-img create on /mnt/mxfs produced no output within its 60 s budget, and the create's real acquire (P-UNPUB-OWNED-META n=64 comm=qemu-img) went through at the moment the resumed victim's mount was taken away.
defects.evidence: 0.89.90 (srcversion B1B7E538F9F908076707471, packaged rpm, RHEL 9.8 5.14.0-687.49.1.el9_8, alma9-1 survivor / alma9-2 victim), tests/evidence/full_verify_0.89.90.log: tcp_peer_freeze_death VERDICT PASS at 00:46:04 CDT, then selinux_svirt 'RESULT FAIL: over the 60 s budget' at 00:47:05 with an empty svirt.log (not even the line printed after qemu-img create). Survivor dmesg tests/evidence/tcp_peer_freeze_death/20260925T004000/dmesg_alma9-1.log: recovery complete t=232.7, P164-DEAD-REJECT of 708001876 t=457.3, P-UNPUB-OWNED-META comm=qemu-img t=538.73, XFS unmount t=539.0 (the chain's unmount of both nodes), 'TCP peer 708001876 closed after clean departure' t=539.37. The same sequence took 5 s on 0.89.88 and 0.89.89 (one run each). Not reproduced in 6 further laps on the same build: 2 probes-off (tests/evidence/repro_svirt_stall_0.89.90.log, create 17 and 25 ms) and 4 with dyndbg=+p (repro_svirt_stall_probes_0.89.90.log, create 42-49 ms). Ruled out: the retired identity's session being present (it is present at unmount in every run, passing ones included); ausearch cost (6.6 ms on the same audit logs). The failing run is the only one that followed the RHEL packaged round, which reboots the pair (node up 9 min).  FURTHER LAPS: 2 in the full failing order (packaged rhel9 round with its reboot, then tcp_peer_freeze_death, then selinux_svirt_mxfs; tests/evidence/repro_svirt_stall_fullorder_0.89.90.log): both PASS, create 20 and 28 ms, so a fresh reboot does not bring it back by itself. 1 more after the watchdog was added (tests/evidence/svirt_watchdog_check_0.89.90.log): PASS in 5 s. Rate on 0.89.90: 1 stall in 10 attempts.  0.89.91 SESSION: 12 more full-order laps on 0.89.90 by tests/svirt_stall_laps.sh (tests/evidence/svirt_stall_laps_0.89.90_20260925T071017.log): all PASS, create 46-164 ms; 3 more with the fixed harnesses (svirt_stall_laps_0.89.90_20260925T090035.log): all PASS. Rate on 0.89.90: 1 stall in 25. TIMING CORRECTION: the create's grant at t=538.73 falls between the SELinux test's ssh being killed at its 60 s budget (00:47:05) and the survivor's own unmount (539.0), and 0.6 s BEFORE the victim departed (539.37) -- it is not tied to the victim's mount going away. During the stall the survivor's 1 s sampler and a PR-IN on the LUN every 2 s both answered without a gap (tcp_peer_freeze_death/20260925T004000 deathworker/prkeys logs), so the node and the SCSI path were live. CANDIDATE MECHANISM, NOT PROVEN FOR THE FAILING RUN: the test's ausearch ran without --input-logs, so it read its stdin (an ssh pipe) and blocks for as long as the caller's stdin stays open (probe: open 25 s pipe held it 24.8 s; /dev/null 6 ms); killing the ssh closes that pipe, which would release it exactly at the budget. But every lap launched as this session's are gets stdin /dev/null (read from /proc/<pid>/fd/0), where it cannot block, and the failing run's stdin cannot be recovered. ausearch now runs with --input-logs </dev/null, which removes that mechanism, so a recurrence under the fixed harness is an MXFS wait. ===== 0.89.93 (packages dist/0.89.93, fixed harnesses): 14 more full-order laps, all PASS, create 76-157 ms (tests/evidence/svirt_stall_laps_0.89.93_20260926T032922.log; the batch was stopped at lap 15 when the session ended). Rate across all attempts: 1 stall in 39, none since the harness's ausearch and instrument-leak fixes (28 laps since them).
defects.next: Reproduce in the full order (packaged rhel9 round with its reboot, then tcp_peer_freeze_death, then selinux_svirt_mxfs; tests/evidence/repro_svirt_stall_fullorder_0.89.90.log) with per-step timestamps (the harness now prints t_start/t_avc/t_mkdir/t_rm/t_create); if it recurs, capture the survivor's blocked stacks (/proc/<pid>/stack of qemu-img) and the DLM lock the create waits on before the budget expires, then A/B against the 0.89.89 packages in dist/0.89.89. ===== tests/selinux_svirt_mxfs.sh now records, 8 s before its budget, the kernel stacks of every D-state task and of qemu-img/mkdir/rm/ausearch on the node into stacks.log, so the next occurrence names the wait. A/B against 0.89.89 needs many laps per build at a 1-in-10 rate. ===== The harness mechanism is removed, so any recurrence now points at MXFS: tests/svirt_stall_laps.sh stops at the first stall with stacks.log (D-state tasks, qemu-img/mkdir/rm) and both nodes' dmesg captured before any unmount. Run it in batches alongside other RHEL work; if it recurs, read the stack for the lock the create waits on, then A/B against dist/0.89.89. Disposition needs a stall caught with its stack: harness-only (disproved) or an MXFS wait (fix). ===== USER DECISION 2026-09-26: the user accepts shipping 0.90.0 with this record open (a ~60 s stall observed once in 39 attempts). It stays in the queue. The ausearch-stdin candidate does not fit the failing run: it was launched as a background tool command, and those get stdin /dev/null (measured 2026-09-26 on the 0.90.0 gate's full_verify pid), so ausearch got EOF at once and could not block. Cause unknown; the next step is still stall laps with the stack capture. ===== 2026-09-28 (4-node release adjudication): impact set to noblock so the ledger's --release answer matches the user's 2026-09-26 ruling recorded above and the record's own timing evidence (self-resolving stall). Not a disposition; the stall laps with stack capture remain the next step.
defects.impact_why: The record's own timing correction shows the stalled create was granted at t=538.73, 0.6 s before the victim departed and before any unmount, so the ~60 s stall resolved by itself: a pace event, not a hang, and no data was lost; the node and its SCSI path answered throughout. defects.summary: A CAW waiter behind a live holder makes the holder receive a blocking notification roughly 13 times a second for the whole wait: 20,164 P7B-BASTNOTIFY for one inode across a 1587 s wait. TCP bounds the same cost with a per-wait notification budget of one re-fire per 10 s (tests/live_holder_wait.sh asserts it); CAW has none, so a long drain costs the holder CPU and log volume in proportion to its length rather than to the number of waits.
defects.evidence: 0.89.92 (7B93190B44BF84F1115F74E), 2/cawd on the QNAP LUN, tests/evidence/20260926T060926Z_livewait_caw0912_s3: test1 held ino 181 with its release paused 1560 s, and test2 read it. Holder P7B-BASTNOTIFY ino=181 = 20164 over W's 1587 s wait. The 540 s control (20260926T055926Z_livewait_caw0912_s2) received 6925 over 547 s, the same ~12.7 per second. Neither lap had a correctness failure: both reads returned the holder's bytes, with no shutdown and no splat.
defects.next: Find where the CAW waiter raises the notification (the slot poll on each P-WAIT-EXTEND lap vs a per-attempt raise) and whether the holder's bast work re-queues per notification. Measure the holder's CPU and log volume during a long drain. Bound it the way TCP does (re-fire interval) if the per-notification cost is real. ===== MECHANISM READ (0.89.93): caw_wait_for_grant re-sends the UDP BAST hint every MXFS_CAW_BAST_RESEND_MS=100 ms for as long as it is blocked (dlm/dlm_caw.c, the v0.5.3 resend; dlm_caw.h:117), and the holder logs P7B-BASTNOTIFY per hint it processes (xfs/xfs_mxfs_bast.c). The cadence is deliberate and measured: most waits are under 100 ms, and a lost packet otherwise waits for the 4 s relaxed disk poll. A faster cadence regressed cc@32 from 60 s to 84-91 s (the comment at the resend site). PROPOSED SHAPE, not made: keep 100 ms for the first few seconds of a wait, then back the resend off exponentially to about 1 s. A wait that old is already a drain the holder knows about, and 1 s bounds lost-hint recovery well under the disk poll. VERIFY with the cc@32 and 2-node create/rsync benches unchanged, plus a live_holder_wait CAW lap showing the holder's per-wait notification count falling to about 1/s. ===== ===== 2026-10-17 (session 41) CHANGE WRITTEN, NOT YET BUILT OR MEASURED. dlm/dlm_caw.c caw_wait_for_grant: the UDP BAST hint re-send keeps MXFS_CAW_BAST_RESEND_MS (100 ms) for the first MXFS_CAW_BAST_RESEND_BACKOFF_AFTER_MS (3000 ms) of a wait, then doubles its interval at each send up to MXFS_CAW_BAST_RESEND_MAX_MS (1000 ms, dlm/dlm_caw.h); same-build switch caw_bast_resend_backoff (default 1, 0 = flat 100 ms, the control). Instrument: P-ACQ-STUCK (every 8 s of an inode wait past 15 s) now ends 'hints=<re-sends so far> hint_ms=<current interval>' (bast_resends was counted and never printed). OPEN QUESTION the A/B answers: the holder logs P7B-BASTNOTIFY per arrival from any source, and its own contention disk poll runs at MXFS_CAW_BAST_POLL_FAST_MS (100 ms) while it sees the waiter's bit, so the measured 12.7/s may be partly the holder's poll, not the waiter's re-send. defects.summary: At 3+ nodes on TCP a clean unmount that runs while the SB summary page's master is a dead peer under recovery fails its final SB summary sync fast (P-SB-SUMMARY-LOCK rc=-107: the request to the dead-in-view master is retried on the transport about ten times over 5 s and the transport error returned) and departs DIRTY (P-SB-SUMMARY-FINAL-FAIL, P-SB-SEAL-DIRTY-DEPARTURE, slot and PR key retained), so a node that quiesced cleanly is fenced and replayed by its peers. At 2 nodes the survivor masters the page after the death and its lock waits on the recovery instead, which is what chain 116's holderfail arm expects.
defects.evidence: Chain 116 holderfail1 at 4/tcp on build 20491955C95C1F9F6A5DE63, tests/evidence/sess475_chain116_d0133_s4e_4tcp.log, captures tests/evidence/sess475_chain116_dmesg_s4e_4tcp/holderfail1_test4.txt: X=test3 parked inside the SB summary critical section (slot 3, epoch 2, sb_summary_bast_refuse=1) and destroyed; Y=test4's unmount logged 'P-SB-SUMMARY-LOCK slot=1 rc=-107 epoch=0 master_self=0 at=put_super', 'P-SB-SUMMARY-FINAL-FAIL slot=1 lock_rc=-107 cover_rc=0 — departure DIRTY', 'P-SB-SEALED slot=1 epoch=0 late_dirty=1', 'P-SB-SEAL-DIRTY-DEPARTURE slot=1'; umount wall 71 s rc=0; peers recovered X (peers_recovered_x=1); chk errors=0. The arm's three 2-node expectations failed: Y took the lock after the holder died, Y's epoch > X's, Y recounted fresh and sealed clean. Mechanism read in dlm/dlm.c (mxfs_dlm_lock_retries): a request whose master is dead but still in the view takes the remote path; the loop retries -ENOTCONN/-EPIPE/-ECONNRESET with a 500 ms sleep while retries > 1 and returns the transport error on the last attempt; the dead member leaves the view only when its recovery completes (about 60 s here). The normal laps of the same chain (fleet unmount, no death) took the lock rc=0 on all four nodes.
defects.next: Design question before any patch: should a request to a dead-in-view master wait for that member's recovery — bounded by it, with the recovery-blocked deny (P-RBLK-DENY-DEAD-MASTER, and since 0.90.12 P-RBLK-DENY-DEAD-AUTHORITY) as the exit for a recovery that cannot complete — instead of failing after the transport retries? If yes, the wait belongs in mxfs_dlm_lock_retries' transport-error branch keyed on dlm_authority_dead of the master, and the holderfail arm of tests/sess475_chain116_d0133_sb_seal.sh at N>2 is the verification (Y must take the lock after X's recovery, epoch > X's, recount + seal clean; the arm's assertions stay as they are). Read the 4/cawd chain (s4e lap 3) for the same arm first: on CAW the summary lock is a slot CAS with no master, so the shape may not exist there.
defects.impact_why: The departure is scored DIRTY and recovered by a peer exactly as a crash would be: Y's unmount returned rc=0 in 71 s (no hang), no shutdown, chk errors=0 after the peers' recovery, no data lost; the cost is a fence and a replay of a log that had already quiesced.

defects.summary: A clean unmount of every node at once leaves lock records in the TCP authority ledger: a release is re-sent ten times and then dropped, and the masters it is addressed to are themselves leaving, so exclusive inode records and shared holder bits of mounts that ended cleanly stay on the platter. They are retired or answered for only when their page is next imported; records on inodes nothing asks for outlive whole mounted eras.
defects.evidence: tests/quiesce_remount_access.sh at 4/tcp, cold census after a four-way unmount (tools/tauth_page_auth.py --holders): 0.90.18 base18a 39 exclusive records; 0.90.21 fifteen laps 0 to 478 records per lap, e.g. v21c_lap5 353 records on 349 pages (346 exclusive, 7 shared bits on slots 1, 2, 3); 125 to 242 records per lap were still on the platter at the second census, all on inodes nothing had asked for. Two origins are established by reading the code and one by measurement: a wire release is dropped after its re-sends (measured), and a view change landing during a local release's commit still ends that release as a remaster (dlm_txn_finalize), which the 0.90.18 stale-image retry narrows and does not close.
defects.next: 1. Count which of the two origins each leftover record comes from: on the departing nodes, P-TAUTH-RELEASE-UNACKED and the dropped-release counter against P-TAUTH-COMMIT-STALE-IMAGE, per lap. 2. For the dropped wire release: a departing node that still holds grants when its masters are leaving has to hand them to whoever writes the page last; the last member to leave masters every page and can retire the records of members that said goodbye before its own GOODBYE. 3. For the local release: when the page stays this node's, finalize keeps the entry PENDING_RELEASE for the re-drive tick, and a departing last member drives such entries synchronously before its GOODBYE. 4. Verify with the census: zero records after a four-way unmount over 12 laps. ===== 2026-10-17 census on build BE8BD4A29D991A268D9B3FA (0.90.83 no-give-up release in it), tests/quiesce_remount_access.sh at 4/net/mesh/direct g4 (needs MXFS_NODE_LIST=test3,test4,test5,test6 on the pooled rig): q131m01 census1=77, q131m02 census1=381 records after a four-way unmount (fails=0). The bar in next step 4 (zero records over 12 laps) is not met: the 0.90.83 change does not close this; next steps 2-3 (last member retires departed members' records; synchronous re-drive before GOODBYE) stand. Log tests/evidence/qra_q131_chain.log.
defects.impact_why: Measured on 0.90.21 over 15 laps of tests/quiesce_remount_access.sh at 4/tcp (30 four-way remounts): zero lock timeouts, zero refused locks, zero hung tasks, zero shutdowns, every access step inside its 30 s bound and every mount under 10 s, with 0 to 478 leftover records per lap on the platter. The records cost a read of the heartbeat table and one page transition when their page is imported; nothing waits behind them since 0.90.21 retires the holders that left for good and 0.90.22 names the tenant for a shared bit on an occupied slot.

defects.summary: After two nodes are power-cut together under a shared-directory load at 8 nodes on TCP, every survivor's load makes no progress for 73-186 s before resuming; the stall is cluster-wide (all six survivors within 1-2 s of each other) and far past what any recovery step should cost.
defects.evidence: multi_victim_containment 8/tcp victims test3,test6, VICTIM_GAP=75 PROVER_HOLD_MS=8000, survivors' load_longest_stall: w35a laps a-f (0.90.35) 184-185, 74-77, 105-110, 73-150, 181-182, 181-185 s; x36b p1 (0.90.36) 184-185 s; x36b fixw2 9-12 s. Present with and without REAP_WAIT_MS=400000; every lap also holds the prover 8 s (PROVER_HOLD_MS), an injected delay. Evidence dirs tests/evidence/multi_victim/20260930T04*_8tcp_w35a_* and *_x36b_*.
defects.next: Measure the same lap with no injected holds (PROVER_HOLD_MS=0, REAP_WAIT_MS=0) to separate the injected delay from the recovery's own cost; then name what the survivors' load waits on during the stall (the lock waits' own probes, per survivor, against the recovery phase lines). ===== TIMELINE (x36c lap 2, tests/evidence/multi_victim/20260930T060926Z_8tcp_x36c_2, T0=1790748639): every survivor's load stops at +11 s (the first victim's kill, +12 s) and resumes at +190-193 s. Victim test3 (node 829808213, slot 6): death fence queued on test1 at +76 s (P309-DEATH-FENCE-QUEUED, 64 s after the kill); test7 fenced and SEALED the manifest at +75.8-77.4 s (P236-FENCE-CERTIFIED, P236-FENCE-SEALED); test1's claim at +76.5 s was refused 'manifest is not sealed yet' (P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED) and the replay was rescheduled with delay_ms=30000 (P89-REAP-SCHED why=freplay-fence); it retried at +106.7 s (P-FREPLAY-RETRY), claimed, replayed, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE +112.2 s. Victim test6 (node 2768476333, slot 3): killed +88 s, P164-DEAD-NOTE +143.8-145.8 s, same refusal at +152.6 s, retry +183.0 s, complete +188.3 s. Meanwhile the survivors' rm/rsync sit in P-ACQ-UNREACHABLE-MASTER-WAIT/NOQUEUE on resources the dead node mastered (179 NOQUEUE on test7). So each victim costs ~60 s of death detection plus ~29 s of a fixed 30 s retry that the seal arriving 1-2 s after the refusal does not cut short. NEXT: have the seal (or a claim refused only for want of it) re-drive the replay immediately instead of the 30 s reap delay; then measure the death-detection share against its design timeout. ===== WHERE THE 30 s COMES FROM (source read, not yet changed): a replayer whose claim is refused with -EPERM (dlm/disklock.c:10433-10445 P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED; dlm/v5_mount.c:15276-15280 returns -EPERM with MXFS_RBLK_NO_CERTIFICATE when the attempt's holder is live) falls through the reclassify in mxfs_dlm_foreign_replay_work_fn (xfs/xfs_mxfs_recovery.c:1380-1395) to set MXFS_REAPF_FREPLAY and mxfs_reap_sched(mp, MXFS_REAP_RETRY_MS, "freplay-fence") (:1397-1408), MXFS_REAP_RETRY_MS a #define 30000 (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm_priv.h:895); the only re-arm is mxfs_freplay_retry_worker (xfs/xfs_mxfs_evict.c:889-912). The prover's seal (mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_seal, dlm/disklock.c:9889) is one durable CAS with no wire message or wakeup, and survivors have no path that observes it (the heartbeat monitor's FENCED read at dlm/disklock.c:3507-3553 only declares a missed death). CHANGE TO MAKE: when the refusal is the live-prover SNAPSHOTTING wait (manifest not yet sealed), re-arm the retry at ~1 s doubling to the 30 s cap instead of 30 s flat; measure with the same two-victim lap (predict load_longest_stall falls by ~25-29 s per victim, P-FREPLAY-RETRY count rises by a handful). ===== 2026-10-18 (session 87) BOTH OF THE MEASURED WAITS HAVE CHANGED IN THE TREE; H-2V1 WRITTEN, ITS A/B QUEUED. Read: (1) the freplay-fence re-arm after a refused claim (xfs/xfs_mxfs_recovery.c, 'NOT replayed -- no proven exclusion') is now mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_wait_ms(ctx, slot, MXFS_REAP_RETRY_MS) (dlm/v5_mount.c): MXFS_RECOV_WAIT_FAST_MS 1000 while a live peer holds the fencing attempt at stage FENCING or SNAPSHOTTING and the wait is younger than MXFS_RECOV_WAIT_FAST_SPAN_MS 20000, the 30 s idle interval otherwise (its comment cites the same shape on 8/disk/caw/mpath path_fenced_return: claim met SNAPSHOTTING, next claim 30.2 s later, stall 120.7 s); (2) on a SCSI attachment the dead window is MXFS_DISKLOCK_SCSI_DEAD_THRESHOLD 17 x 2 s = 34 s (dlm/disklock.h, derived from the 30 s authority lease plus the fence's exclusion), not the 62 s of 0.90.36. HYPOTHESIS H-2V1: the record's stall was those two fixed waits; each victim now costs the 34 s window plus its observation start plus fence, seal and replay, with no fixed 30 s wait. Queue tests/queues/twovictim_fastretry_8tcp.queue (8/net/mesh/direct g8, victims test9,test12, VICTIM_GAP=75; P laps production, H laps PROVER_HOLD_MS=8000), rules in its header written before the first lap: SUPPORTED when every lap PASS, every DETECT <= 40 s, FENCE+REPLAY <= 15 s, an H lap reaches a refusal and its re-arms read delay_ms=1000 with recovery within 5 s of the seal; REFUTED by a 30000 ms re-arm with a live holder younger than 20 s, a recovery >= 25 s after its seal, or DETECT > 40 s.
